title: Natural selection and adaptation
blurb: Explain how natural selection changes a population, tell it apart from drift, gene flow and Lamarck's rejected idea, and read the evidence for evolution.
question: After years of heavy antibiotic use in one hospital, most of the bacteria of one species there are resistant to the drug. Did the antibiotic cause the resistance, or did something else happen? And why do biologists say populations evolve, not individuals?

teach.body: Formal definition: evolution is a change in the inherited traits (allele frequencies) of a population over generations. Natural selection, described by Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace, is the main mechanism that makes populations better suited to their environment. Plain English: individuals do not evolve during their lives. A population evolves when the individuals with helpful inherited traits leave more offspring, so those traits become more common generation after generation.

teach.caption: Mutation is the original source of new alleles; crossing over, independent assortment and random fertilization reshuffle them.

teach.body: Fitness is reproductive success: the number of surviving, fertile offspring an individual leaves, not its strength or size. An adaptation is an inherited trait (structural, physiological or behavioral) that raises fitness in a particular environment. Adaptations come from variation that already exists; organisms do not grow a trait because they need it. Traits acquired during life, such as muscles built by training, are not inherited: that was Lamarck's idea, and it was rejected.

teach.body: Marisol, a nursing applicant working as a lab assistant, reads a report on drug-resistant bacteria. Before the antibiotic was used, a few bacteria already carried resistance alleles from random mutations. The drug killed the susceptible cells; the resistant ones survived and divided. Repeated over many generations, the population became mostly resistant. The antibiotic did not cause the mutations: it selected bacteria that already had them. That is natural selection observed directly.

teach.text: Exam traps: individuals do NOT evolve, populations do; organisms do not develop traits because they need them; acquired traits are NOT inherited; fitness means reproductive success, not strength; antibiotics SELECT resistance, they do not cause it; drift is random while selection is not; homologous = same structure, analogous = same job.

items: Evolution: change in a population's allele frequencies over generations.
Natural selection: variation, heritability, overproduction, differential reproduction, change.
Fitness = reproductive success. Adaptation = inherited trait that raises fitness.
Mutation is the original source of new alleles; selection sorts existing variation.
Drift (random, small populations), gene flow (migration), sexual and artificial selection.
Evidence: fossils, homologous structures, embryology, DNA, biogeography, observed resistance.

summary: You can now describe the steps of natural selection, define fitness and adaptation, and tell selection apart from genetic drift, gene flow and Lamarck's rejected idea. You can also name the three patterns of selection and the main lines of evidence for evolution, including homologous and analogous structures.

A.q: In evolutionary biology, an organism's fitness is measured by its:
A.why: Fitness is reproductive success: how many surviving, fertile offspring an individual leaves.

whyNot.0: Strength and speed matter only if they lead to more offspring.
whyNot.2: A long life with few offspring still means low fitness.
whyNot.3: Size is not fitness unless it increases reproductive success.

A.q: Which pair of structures is homologous?
options: A bird wing and a bee wing
A bat wing and a moth wing
A human arm and a bat wing
A fly wing and a sparrow wing
A.why: The human arm and bat wing share the same underlying bones from a common ancestor, though they do different jobs.

whyNot.0: Bird and bee wings share a function but not an origin: they are analogous.
whyNot.1: Bat and moth wings evolved separately for flight: analogous.
whyNot.3: Insect and bird wings are built from different structures: analogous.

A.q: What is the original source of the new alleles on which natural selection acts?
A.why: Mutation creates new alleles; selection and drift change how common existing alleles are.

whyNot.0: Natural selection sorts variation that already exists; it does not create alleles.
whyNot.1: Genetic drift changes allele frequencies by chance but creates no new alleles.
whyNot.2: Artificial selection is human-chosen breeding, which also sorts existing variation.

B.q: A student says giraffes got long necks because each generation stretched to reach leaves and passed the longer neck on. Which idea is this?
options: Genetic drift in a small herd
B.why: Passing on a trait gained by use during life is Lamarck's inheritance of acquired characteristics, which was rejected.

whyNot.1: Natural selection works on neck lengths that already vary at birth, not on stretching.
whyNot.2: Genetic drift is a random change in allele frequencies, not a trait gained by effort.
whyNot.3: Gene flow is the movement of alleles by migration between populations.

B.q: A few birds blown to a remote island start a new population whose allele frequencies differ from the mainland's by chance. What is this called?
B.why: When a few individuals found a new population, chance decides which alleles they carry: the founder effect, a form of genetic drift.

whyNot.0: Stabilizing selection favors average traits; this change happened by chance.
whyNot.2: Gene flow is ongoing migration between populations; the island birds are now cut off.
whyNot.3: Artificial selection is breeding chosen by humans.

B.q: In one seed-eating bird, individuals with small or large beaks survive better than those with medium beaks. Which type of selection is this?
B.why: Disruptive selection favors both extremes over the average, widening the range of the trait.

whyNot.0: Directional selection favors one extreme, not both.
whyNot.1: Stabilizing selection favors the average, the opposite of this case.
whyNot.3: Artificial selection is human-chosen breeding; here survival in nature decides.

C.q: A bacterial infection returns after treatment and no longer responds to the same antibiotic. Which statement best explains this change?
options: The drug caused the surviving bacteria to mutate.
Each bacterium adapted to the drug during treatment.
The patient's immune cells made the bacteria resistant.
Bacteria already resistant survived and multiplied.
C.why: Resistance alleles existed before treatment. The drug removed susceptible bacteria, so the resistant ones left most of the offspring.

whyNot.0: The antibiotic does not cause mutations; it selects bacteria that already had them.
whyNot.1: Individual bacteria do not adapt because they need to; the population changes by selection.
whyNot.2: Immune cells destroy bacteria; they do not give them resistance alleles.

C.q: Which observation shows evolution happening within a human lifetime?
options: Insects becoming resistant to a pesticide
Similar bone patterns in mammal forelimbs
Older fossils found in deeper rock layers
Similar early embryos in fish and humans
C.why: Pesticide resistance spreading through insect populations over a few years is evolution observed directly.

whyNot.1: Homologous forelimbs are evidence of common ancestry long ago, not change seen today.
whyNot.2: The fossil record shows change over very long periods of the past.
whyNot.3: Similar embryos point to shared ancestry, not to change within a lifetime.

C.q: Which statement about evolution is accurate?
options: An individual's genes change to suit its habitat.
A population's allele frequencies change over time.
Selection produces the traits that a species needs.
Traits gained by practice pass to the offspring.
C.why: Evolution is a change in the allele frequencies of a population across generations.

whyNot.0: Individuals do not evolve; their genes do not change to fit the environment.
whyNot.2: Selection acts on variation that already exists; it does not produce needed traits.
whyNot.3: Acquired traits are not inherited (Lamarck's idea was rejected).

reteach.title: Sifting gravel
reteach.question: A gardener shakes mixed gravel through a sieve. How is the sieve like the environment in natural selection?

blocks.h: The sieve does not make pebbles
blocks.body: A load of gravel already holds pebbles of many sizes: that is variation. Shaking it through a sieve keeps the pebbles that fit and loses the rest. The sieve never shapes a pebble to fit; it only sorts what is already there. Now imagine the kept pebbles could "breed" more pebbles like themselves: the next load would be mostly the kept size. The environment is the sieve, and inherited traits are the pebble sizes.

blocks.text: The sieve never changes a pebble. An antibiotic never creates resistance: it sorts the bacteria that already had it.

explain.body: Natural selection needs heritable variation, more offspring than can survive, and differences in survival and reproduction. Without inherited differences there is nothing to select.

test.q: Which condition must be present for natural selection to occur?
options: A need felt by organisms to adapt
test.why: Selection can act only on differences that are inherited.

whyNot.1: Needs do not create traits; variation must exist first.
whyNot.2: Identical offspring would leave nothing to select.
whyNot.3: Acquired traits are not inherited, so selection cannot pass them on.

explain.body: An adaptation is an inherited trait that improves survival and reproduction in a given environment. A change gained during one life (a tan, trained muscles, a scar) is not inherited and is not an adaptation in the evolutionary sense.

test.q: Which is an adaptation in the evolutionary sense?
options: Muscles built by a sled dog's training
A tan gained from the summer sun
A thick coat inherited by arctic foxes
A scar left by an old fight injury
test.why: The fox's thick coat is inherited and raises survival in the cold, so it is an adaptation.

whyNot.0: Trained muscles are acquired during life and are not inherited.
whyNot.1: A tan is acquired from sun exposure and is not inherited.
whyNot.3: A scar is acquired damage, not an inherited trait.

explain.body: Genetic drift is random change, strongest in small populations (bottleneck and founder effects). Gene flow moves alleles between populations by migration. Selection is the only mechanism that is not random.

test.q: Which mechanism changes allele frequencies by chance and has the strongest effect in small populations?
test.why: Genetic drift is random change in allele frequencies, and chance events matter most when a population is small.

whyNot.0: Natural selection is nonrandom: it favors better-suited individuals.
whyNot.1: Gene flow is the movement of alleles by migration.
whyNot.2: Sexual selection is nonrandom choice of mates.

explain.body: Homologous structures share an underlying structure from a common ancestor; analogous structures share a job but evolved separately; vestigial structures are reduced remnants. DNA similarity, fossils and embryos add more evidence.

test.q: A bird wing and a butterfly wing are best described as:
test.why: They share a function (flight) but are built from different structures, so they evolved separately: analogous.

whyNot.0: Homologous structures share the same underlying anatomy, which these wings do not.
whyNot.2: Vestigial structures are reduced remnants; both wings are fully working.
whyNot.3: Embryonic similarity is a separate line of evidence, not a type of adult structure.
